brief.stakes: PRP has paid around $30M for a 117K SF office building that is roughly 60% vacant. They stand to gain if they can lease up the empty floors and improve the building, but they risk losing if tenant demand doesn't materialize.
brief.tension: The building is roughly 60% vacant, and the seller, Tishman Speyer, had owned it since 2006 and completed a substantial renovation in 2017, yet still couldn't fill it. PRP calls the deal a 'basis reset' and plans to invest six figures into modifications, betting they can succeed where Tishman didn't.
brief.why_now: This deal closed on Tuesday, and it's a concrete example of how investors are approaching distressed office assets in D.C. It also comes as the neighboring International Square's CMBS loans were sent to special servicing and its $450M capital stack matures this month, showing the pressure on office owners.
brief.number_that_matters: 60% vacancy, concentrated on three empty floors of 16K SF each. The building has enough contiguous space for an anchor tenant, but it's been empty despite a 2017 renovation.
brief.lens_note: PRP is buying a building at a 'basis reset' from a seller who had invested in a substantial renovation but still faced 60% vacancy. This reflects a shift in capital flows: new owners with lower basis can afford to reinvest and wait for lease-up, while previous owners may not be interested in further investment.

The buyer completed the acquisition through its TS Plus fund, which has raised $973 million and targets core-plus investments in high-growth markets.
I read the fund's target as a signal: they want a stable property with room to improve, not a passive bet.
Berkshire Dilworth is 97 percent occupied.

It is next to Little Sugar Creek Greenway, a regional trail system connecting Uptown Charlotte with neighborhoods across Mecklenburg County.
The unit mix includes studios and one- to three-bedroom floorplans with an average size of 856 square feet.
The building also includes a penthouse collection.
Interiors feature plank flooring, kitchens with custom cabinetry and islands, bathrooms with soaking tubs and walk-in showers, washers and dryers, walk-in closets and private terraces.

Outdoor offerings include a swimming pool, a sundeck and a terrace lounge.
The community also includes a pet spa, EV charging stations, 395 parking spots and 3,000 square feet of street-level retail.

At the end of the first quarter of 2026, developers had 24,927 units underway across the metro, while another 96,000 units were in the planning and permitting stages, according to a recent Yardi Matrix report.

brief.protagonist: UWM Holdings Corp., and by extension its CEO Mat Ishbia
brief.stakes: UWM is trying to stay the dominant mortgage lender while its balance sheet has deteriorated: equity nearly halved, leverage more than tripled, and it just swung to a $451.9 million quarterly loss. The $2.05 billion capital partnership is a lifeline, but it comes with suspended dividends and new board seats for Oaktree.
brief.tension: UWM is leaning into growth while its financial footing has weakened. It lost a bid for Two Harbors, analysts flagged its leverage, and now it must answer to a powerful credit investor. Ishbia frames it as strength; the numbers frame it as necessity.
brief.why_now: The capital raise and Q2 results were announced together this week, showing a market leader making a high-stakes balance-sheet pivot in public.
brief.number_that_matters: $451.9 million net loss in Q2, compared with a $170.4 million profit the prior quarter. That reversal, attributed to a hedge-related event tied to the failed Two Harbors deal, is the wound the new capital is meant to treat.
brief.lens_note: UWM is at the point in the cycle where growth ambitions collide with leverage, forcing a capital raise, dividend suspension, and deleveraging. The deal shows how even top players must pay up for permanence when the cycle turns.
